A variant where the Haar wavelet decomposition is used for noise removal.
Thresholding is applied to eliminate detail coefficients below a certain value, preserving significant image details while removing noise.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$ for a single pass, where $N$ is the number of data points.
Each pass reduces the data size by half (in each dimension), so subsequent passes are faster.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ to store the original and all detail coefficients.
The approximation coefficients are a subset of the original size.
*   **Limitations:** The step-function nature of the Haar wavelet leads to blocky artifacts in the reconstructed signal compared to smoother wavelets (e.g., Daubechies).
It is less suitable for data requiring smooth transitions.
*   **When not to use:** When smoothness is required or when the data has complex high-frequency structures that the Haar wavelet cannot capture well.
The Haar wavelet transform is one of the earliest wavelet transforms, developed by Alfred Haar in 1910.
It is defined by Monet Morlet [Parent] to avoid the fixed resolution limit of windowed Fourier transforms.
It decomposes the signal into a family of functions, which are the translation and dilation of unique $\psi(x)$ [Parent].
